comments.author: alexpotato
comments.text: A couple points: 1. Random knowledge can often be used to build a "map" to conclusions that turn out to be useful e.g. someone once asked me what what country was number 2 in terms of total airplane flights (the US is number 1). I deduced: - had to be a big country - with spread out cities - and required flying instead of driving I remembered reading that Brazil has traffic that is so bad and such poor security that people commute to work via helicopter. Even though I wasn't sure it was Brazil, I could guesstimate that it was indeed Brazil. 2. Random facts are great for creating shared references or metaphors across cultural or organizational boundaries. e.g. I worked with many people from India over the years and being able to quote a famous Bollywood movie or Indian mythology was excellent at helping build rapport etc 3. I was watching a documentary on an Army jungle survival school. The instructor mentioned: "People ask me if they should read survival guides or biographies of people who survived a calamity. I 100% say yes b/c the after action reports of people surviving are filled with stories of 'then I remembered this random fact from years ago that helped me survive'."

comments.author: gumby
comments.text: It's great that it has such a lineage and is still around, but according to its history it was a bbs / netnews login host. World.std.com was providing internet access in 89 or 90 by log in, and of course many universities by then had hordes of people dialing up, logging in, and using the net; A similar BBS->net hybrid was the Well. Pobably The Little Garden (later TLGNet) in 1990 was the first ISP in the sense it's used today: there were no user hosts that you logged into and then ran programs; it literally only provided IP service and you had to have a router to connect. We gave instructions on how to make a router with KA9Q and and an old PC, to those who needed it. Fun trivia: the first person who managed TLG full time (before that it was just a spinoff of Cygnus, with its first POP my spare bedroom) was Tom Jennings, the author of FIDONET one of the Ur-BBS systems, and surely the biggest. There are a lot of folks from that time on HN. PS: the name The Little Garden came from my favorite restaurant back then, a famous hacker hangout where folks from PARC, Stanford, SRI, Sun etc would hang out. Gosper was a regular.

comments.author: hazrmard
comments.text: Perplexity is not defined in the article. FYI: Perplexity is the degree of surprise the model has in predicting the next token, over a sequence of tokens. At the worst case, perplexity is equal to the size of the vocabulary. At the best case, perplexity is 1. So, given a sequence of tokens, "e = m c ^ 2", if the p(token | prev tokens) = 1 for every token, perplexity ends up being 1. If, however, it's a random predictor, the p(token | prev tokens) is 1/vocab for every token, and perplexity ends up being len(vocab). The article plots log(perplexity) on the y-axis, which puts the best case at 0 (i.e. log 1).

comments.author: jrflo
comments.text: This trend is pretty shocking to me. I assumed that we had moved beyond cross-entropy loss being important with the increasing use of RL, it's wild that the trend is so clear. Really nice to have such a simple benchmark instead of the increasingly convoluted ones that are getting spun up every day. Also, I wonder what happened with GPT 4.5? I think o1 was the start of true reasoning models, right? I was using Claude at the time so I can't remember.

comments.author: d_burfoot
comments.text: The perplexity / intelligence correspondence is one of those ideas that is surprising at first, but in retrospect could not work any other way. The "magic" of intelligence is the ability to extract sophisticated world models from large volumes of raw sensor data. The prediction (=compression) rate on the raw data stream is exactly the metric that captures this progress. I argued this point in a 2008 paper: https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-540-69134-1_... I elaborated on this idea in my 2011 book: https://arxiv.org/abs/1104.5466 I used the word "reusability" to express the idea that the world models obtained via the large scale data compression task could be repurposed for other tasks. (So, Burfoot, if you were so prescient, why aren't you a rich and famous frontier lab researcher? The answer is: I did not think neural nets would scale up).

comments.author: BenoitEssiambre
comments.text: If you like perplexity, I've long advocated for using equivalent ideas when evaluating code and engineering quality. https://benoitessiambre.com/entropy.html It's fundamental to anything trying to be smart. The fact that LLMs explicitly target this measure is one reason they are getting good at engineering and architecture, sometimes better than humans who think they know better but lean on engineering fads instead of more mathematically supported (but more nuanced and probabilistic) principles like entropy/perplexity.

comments.text: Microsoft is now signing on to this effort to measure and potentially limit their base model perplexities, see this tweet from Mustafa Suleyman adding the MAI models to the chart: https://x.com/mustafasuleyman/status/2124663594449318173 > We're committed to sharing our pre-training progress on a common held-out evaluation set. With OpenAI's permission, we report MAI-2 Base on their evaluation set. Its log-perplexity is 0.819, putting it in the same ballpark as the GPT-5.6 Sol base model. comments.text: I think bloggers should mostly write how they feel like. Yes, there’s an audience, or a potential audience, but you calculate how much you want to optimize for the audience and how much to optimize for other qualities. comments.author: Animats
comments.text: Attempts at governance are futile until we recognize that we have built a machine and set it on its course. Instead, we pretend that the market is a natural phenomenon best left alone, and we fail to hold its mechanism designers to account. We need to tear down and rebuild that machine, reprogramming it so that human flourishing, not corporate profit, becomes its goal. This article has useful insights. It points out that capitalism is an optimization engine for something. Shareholder value and CEO compensation, mostly. It reminds us of something that many people would prefer be forgotten - capitalism operates under rules set by governments, and those shape the market. Tax law matters - what's deductible warps spending patterns. Bankruptcy law matters - who gets left holding the bag? Corporation law matters - how immune are executives from the consequences of their decisions? Labor law matters - do people go to jail for wage and hour law violations? All of those are changeable by legislation. Most have become much more favorable to companies since 1970. That's not necessarily permanent. We had a New Deal in the 1930s, following the Gilded Age of the 1920s and the crash of 1929.

comments.author: michalsustr
comments.text: It’s a long article, and the most important idea is buried towards the end: > That’s where I come back to the idea of mechanism design as reverse game theory. Rather than asking ourselves the rules of the game we are now playing, it calls us to ask “What game ought we to be playing?” And that question leads me imperatively to my answer: “The game of human flourishing.” I wholeheartedly agree: we should think way harder about what we want humanity to optimize for collectively, rather than keeping it haphazard. The current economic system is built on the idea of ‘shareholder value maximisation’, which, in a finite world, will ultimately become simply ‘value extraction’. With AI, we’ve built an automated value extractor, which can extract value even faster than was done before. Because of that, the old model can no longer work for improving human flourishing — in a finite world, it will inevitably lead to economic accumulation by few entities, throttling the economic flow.

Now interest rates are back and tech companies are cannibalizing their core competencies on the back of AI. Will markets begin slapping wrists for reckless spending and will upstarts see weakness and stab at exposed bellies? No guarantee they will but it is more possible than analysts are realizing.

comments.author: Murfalo
comments.text: > In my 2005 essay “What Is Web 2.0?” I described how the companies that survived the dotcom bust had all, in one way or another, figured out how to help people navigate the resulting information explosion at scale. As Herbert Simon noted in 1971, an abundance of information leads to a scarcity of attention. In the face of increasing information abundance, he predicted that we would use machines to help us better allocate our time and attention. And so it has transpired: Information has become so abundant that it defies manual curation. Instead, powerful, proprietary algorithmic systems use the data they collect to match users with the answers, news, entertainment, products, applications, and services they seek. Today’s AI is in many ways a continuation of this arc. This is something I've been thinking about a lot. For so long our algorithms have been weaponized against ourselves, but it really feels like we are agonizingly close to finally being able to put them to good use... Couldn't come sooner!

comments.author: Avamander
comments.text: For the price and complexity of building a good Linux-based time server I'd heavily recommend looking at FPGA-based solutions instead. x86 platforms also have PCIe PTM and TGPIO options available[0], which are tad better than the common ARM equivalents and GPIO interrupts. In general Pi-s are relatively bad for timekeeping. Not just the NIC (which can be replaced by hats with their own), there are also oscillator replacement mods[2] to work around this to some extent. Though all this still leaves many other sources of timekeeping error. So if the goal is low-cost precise timekeeping, one can assemble something FPGA-based[2] for quite a bit less money, that can reach very low noise figures. You can spend the remaining money on the GNSS antenna and receiver instead. I'm also sure a FPGA-based approach could be taken even further with some external timekeeping chips available and the FPGA could just do the NTP/PTP protocol stuff. [0]: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zxK0_j2Ah2I [1]: https://raspberrypi.stackexchange.com/questions/74482/switch... [2]: https://fy.chalmers.se/~f96hajo/fakernet/board_Arty_A7-35-GP...

comments.text: There's low-hanging fruit IMHO by testing using semantic naming vocabulary with semantic error vocabulary. Example macro: assert_approx_eq_with_relative_error!(a, b, err). comments.author: rkagerer
comments.text: Way too much caution in this thread. I've done all kinds of programming including embedded and full stack (from before the latter was even a colloquialized term). I absolutely love the degree of control you can get at the microcontroller level. One of my proudest projects had IRQ handlers written in assembly where I counted instruction cycles in order to guarantee worst-case latencies and well-defined impact to realtime activities in the main loop. There were also some lower-priority tasks going on that were cooperatively multitasked. Some time later I wrote a JavaScript library that mimicked some of those cooperative multitasking concepts to queue background image downloads and other generic "ITasks" in a manner that maximally utilized available connections (which were extremely limited by servers back then) and allowed on-the-fly reordering. The frontend used it to always ensure whatever image the user was most interested in (i.e. tiny previews, and large version of the result presently hovered over or that we anticipate will be hovered next) came up as close to instantaneous as we could get, and the rest of the large images lazy-loaded in an intelligent order. The result was an experience that felt so much faster than how most other websites operated back then (and ironically even now as bloat has really slowed a lot of sites down), and users loved it. So the concepts you learn at one end of the spectrum can definitely benefit you at the other. I have much less fun now that so much of the web has moved to React and other cookie cutter frameworks where the level of control comes at a higher cost (in terms of learning curve, understanding all the layers of abstraction, and space for developer creativity). In other words, just get in there and start playing with a personal project or two, and trust your instincts and all the experience that honed them!

comments.text: I'd say just do it. You have been in the industry for 15+ years and you surely know how to network/do interviews. I feel that you are just hesitating or wait for some confirmations. They might have a cousin who actually refers them to the company; They might have worked 10 years of embedded projects as a hobby; They might be lucky because 5 years ago there were a huge opening somewhere. I heard of a metaphor about elevators -- Several people ride an elevator to floor 100, and a reporter asked them how they get there -- one of them said he did 1,000 push-ups, another said he read 2 books, and a third said he bumped his head against the elevator's walls. Those experience might be very well relevant, or not. But above all, copying others' experience, in THIS market, probably doesn't work. comments.author: tptacek
comments.text: I started my career in C/C++ and have done a fair amount of embedded work. In terms of actually doing stuff, there has never in the history of the world been a better time to do low-level and embedded systems work. The right advice here: find a project, scrounge the parts, and have an agent do basic bring-up work for you. If your last serious C work was 15 years ago, I think you'll be astonished how quickly you can progress to the "rewarding" part of any project. If your question is instead how you make a career transition to embedded/firmware work, that's much trickier. The obvious concern is AI's impact on the job market, but I'm chiming in to observe that this isn't the biggest problem with a web->embedded transition. Good jobs doing embedded stuff, at least for people who don't already have a pedigree doing that work, has for as long as I can remember been a bottleneck for people wanting to do this stuff. There's simply a lot more high-level work to be done than low-level work. I can see bright spots potentially ahead; I'm not a big Jevon's Paradox person but one kind of clearly Jevon-y area is hardware, because we've zorched one of the biggest impediments to getting new projects off the ground. But it hasn't happened yet, and might not.

comments.text: Note that if you want to write a programming language, it's not too hard, even doing it from scratch in C without any specific helper libraries. You should try it over a week, it's great fun (the first time). Either make an interpreter or a compiler to another language you're very familiar with - you do not need to understand how to make an executable file. The main technique you probably won't figure out by yourself is called "recursive descent parsing". You can also use a parser generator if you like one.
